name: Procyanidin oral (melasma)

card.summary: An antioxidant pill combo with one small placebo-controlled melasma trial reported, and little else.
card.aka: procyanidin with vitamins A, C, E
card.note: Evidence rests on a single 56-person trial as summarized on Wikipedia.

quick.overview:
This is a supplement combining procyanidin, a plant polyphenol, with vitamins A, C and E, tested for melasma.
One 8-week placebo-controlled trial in 56 women reported improvement on the cheeks. No other studies were found.
quick.mechanism: How it would act is unclear; antioxidant activity is the usual proposed basis for such combinations.
quick.risks: The trial summary describes the regimen as safe and well tolerated. Long-term safety data were not found.

lead: Oral procyanidin combined with vitamins A, C and E is an antioxidant supplement regimen tested for melasma, a condition of brown or gray-brown facial patches. People interested in it want a pill that evens out facial pigmentation from the inside, as a complement to sunscreen and topical lighteners, for a clearer and more uniform complexion.

The main published study is an 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial by Handog and colleagues at the Research Institute for Tropical Medicine in Manila, published in 2009 in the International Journal of Dermatology. It enrolled 60 women with bilateral epidermal melasma (Fitzpatrick skin types III to V), and 56 finished.[2] Instrument readings showed reduced pigmentation in both cheek regions and MASI scores improved, and the regimen was described as safe and well tolerated with minimal adverse events.[2] Wikipedia lists it among oral options for melasma, and a 2023 systematic review of topical and systemic melasma therapies, co-authored by Handog, lists procyanidins among adjunct oral agents alongside Polypodium leucotomos.[1][13]

Procyanidins belong to the proanthocyanidin family of plant polyphenols, found in grape seed, pine bark, cocoa and other foods, and the compounds were identified by French researcher Jacques Masquelier in 1947, who patented extraction methods from pine bark and grape seed, and extracts such as Pycnogenol are sold as supplements.[12] Dermatology reviews describe melasma as a chronic, recurrence-prone condition where no single treatment is universally effective and combinations often perform best.[3]

angle.text: People with melasma take oral antioxidants hoping to lighten cheek patches and even out skin tone. In the one published trial, pigmentation readings and MASI scores on the cheeks improved over eight weeks.

sections.h: Melasma and why oral agents are explored
paras: Melasma is a chronic acquired hypermelanosis characterised by irregular brown macules, symmetrically distributed on sun-exposed areas, particularly the face. It affects mainly women, especially during the reproductive years, and more pigmented phenotypes (Fitzpatrick types III to V); over 40 percent of patients report affected relatives, and triggers include sun exposure, pregnancy, sex hormones, skin inflammation, cosmetics, steroids and photosensitising drugs.[5] Wikipedia describes epidermal and dermal types, with epidermal melanin looking lighter and dermal melanin darker under a Wood's lamp, and notes that recurrence is common, especially in summer.[1]

Reviews of pathogenesis describe changes beyond hyperfunctional melanocytes: alterations of the epidermis, basement membrane and upper dermis, with roles proposed for solar elastosis, mast cells, vascular changes, senescent fibroblasts, visible light and hormones.[6][7] An antioxidant approach is conceptually linked to the roles proposed for oxidative stress and the endogenous antioxidant system in these reviews.[7]

Wikipedia describes proanthocyanidins as oligomeric flavonoids, mostly built from catechin and epicatechin units, with procyanidins as one subgroup and A-type and B-type forms. Jacques Masquelier is credited with discovering them in 1947 and patenting extraction from pine bark and grape seeds.[12]

Per 100 g, Wikipedia lists grape seed at about 3,532 mg, red wine at about 313 mg and cocoa beans as the richest source overall. Pycnogenol, a maritime pine bark extract, is 65 to 75 percent proanthocyanidins, and Wikipedia reports that bioavailability is low, with about 90 percent unabsorbed in the intestine until gut bacteria metabolise it.[12] The same article cites a Cochrane review stating that evidence is insufficient to support Pycnogenol for any chronic disorder, a statement about that product in general rather than melasma.[12]

Oral agents for melasma named by Wikipedia include tranexamic acid, procyanidin with vitamins A, C and E, and, from a systematic review, Polypodium leucotomos extract, beta-carotenoids and melatonin, which the review found effective with few and mild adverse events.[1] Standard care generally centers on topicals, sun avoidance and broad-spectrum sunscreen.[1]

Oral agents are used alongside topical treatments, including hydroquinone, tretinoin, azelaic acid, kojic acid and triple combinations, and procedures such as peels and lasers, which Wikipedia lists for melasma; it also notes that treatments act gradually and are often described as unsatisfying overall.[1] Oral procyanidin is described there as a promising option for epidermal melasma.[1]
Looksmax.org threads on skin lightening and melasma compile treatment lists drawn from review tables, with oral agents such as Polypodium leucotomos appearing among them.[4]

The Handog 2009 trial randomized 60 adult women with bilateral epidermal melasma to oral procyanidin with vitamins A, C and E or placebo, taken twice daily with meals for 8 weeks; 56 completed. Endpoints were pigmentation measured by mexameter, the Melasma Area and Severity Index (MASI), global evaluation by patient and investigator, and safety at each visit. Mexameter readings fell significantly in the left and right malar regions (P < 0.0001) and MASI scores improved in both (P = 0.001), and the authors described the regimen as safe and well tolerated with minimal adverse events.[2] Wikipedia summarizes it as showing significant improvement in the malar regions.[1]

A 2023 systematic review of topical and systemic melasma therapies searched PubMed and EMBASE through May 2021, screened 4,020 articles and included 174 randomized or controlled clinical trials. It recommends oral tranexamic acid when there are no contraindications, and lists procyanidins, Polypodium leucotomos and synbiotics among adjunct oral options.[13] A 2022 systematic review of melasma treatments reports that tranexamic acid and Polypodium leucotomos had promising results, that recurrence is high across treatments, and that combination therapy performed best.[3]

A 2026 systematic review of natural products for melasma, covering 10 randomized trials with MASI or modified MASI as the main outcome, reports that agents including Pycnogenol, lycopene, hydroxytyrosol and Aloe vera reduced scores by 20 to 70 percent, often comparable to 4 percent hydroquinone, with mild adverse events and with small samples, short follow-up and varied formulations noted as limits.[14] Pycnogenol is a related proanthocyanidin product, distinct from the procyanidin-plus-vitamins regimen. The same search shows further 2025 and 2026 publications on antioxidants and melasma, including a cross-sectional study of dietary antioxidant intake in women with facial melasma.[14]

Other randomized trials in melasma have studied different treatments, including a split-face trial of 3% tranexamic acid cream versus 4% hydroquinone in skin of color, a 2025 comparison of oral and topical tranexamic acid, and a 2025 trial of niosomal and conventional tranexamic acid/niacinamide creams versus hydroquinone.[8][9][10] These are separate from the procyanidin regimen, which has one published randomized trial.

Procyanidins are polyphenols described as having antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties; the trial abstract does not itself establish how the regimen reduces pigment.[2][12] Reviews of melasma pathogenesis discuss oxidative stress, the antioxidant system and inflammation as contributors to the hypermelanogenic phenotype, which is the general rationale given for antioxidant supplements.[7]

The trial reported minimal adverse events over eight weeks.[2] Vitamins A, C and E are common supplement ingredients whose total intake from all sources is a consideration, and long-term data on this specific combination have not been published. Oral options for melasma generally are described in a Wikipedia-cited review as having few and mild adverse events.[1]

On looksmax.org oral antioxidants appear in a thread that reproduces a review table of skin-lightening options for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, melasma and general skin lightening, with the original poster directing readers to the adverse-event column; oral Polypodium leucotomos appears in the table.[4] Procyanidin is discussed less than topicals such as hydroquinone and tretinoin.

timeline.event: Jacques Masquelier discovers proanthocyanidins and later patents extraction from pine bark and grape seed.[12]
Handog and colleagues publish an 8-week placebo-controlled trial of oral procyanidin with vitamins A, C and E in Filipino women with melasma.[2]
Systematic review of melasma treatments reports combination therapy performing best and recurrence high.[3]
Systematic review of topical and systemic melasma therapies includes procyanidins among adjunct oral options.[13]
Systematic review of natural products for melasma, including Pycnogenol, reports MASI reductions in 10 randomized trials.[14]

lore.intro: Oral options for melasma and skin lightening are discussed on looksmax.org in lists compiled from review articles, mainly alongside topical agents.[4]

claims.claim: Oral antioxidants can help lighten melasma.
claims.believers: Forum users compile oral and topical lightening options from review tables and choose by side-effect profile.[4]
claims.experts: One small placebo-controlled trial reported lower pigmentation readings on the cheeks with procyanidin plus vitamins A, C and E; no replication has been located.[2]

claims.claim: An oral pill can substitute for sunscreen and topical care in melasma.
claims.believers: Skin-lightening lists place oral agents beside topicals as options.[4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia and reviews describe standard care as centring on sun avoidance, broad-spectrum sunscreen and topicals, with oral agents used alongside.[1][3]

claims.claim: Plant polyphenols such as Pycnogenol lighten pigmentation comparably to hydroquinone.
claims.believers: Proponents of pine bark extract point to its high proanthocyanidin content as the antioxidant basis for skin effects.[12]
claims.experts: A 2026 systematic review of 10 trials reports MASI reductions of 20 to 70 percent with natural products including Pycnogenol, often comparable to 4 percent hydroquinone, while noting small samples and short follow-up.[14]
